passage:
"Before we start, Vinita," Leela said in the Monday team meeting, "I talk too much. Last time I counted: I spoke five times before anyone else got one turn. I'm going to keep count today."
Vinita smiled. "That's honest."
Ten minutes later Leela was mid-flow about the launch plan. She stopped herself. "That's my third turn. Vinita, what do you think? You know the vendor better than I do."
Vinita sat up. "Actually, I think their timeline is optimistic. I've worked with them twice."
"Say more."
Leela nodded, wrote it down and kept quiet till Vinita finished.

qa.q: How many times did Leela speak before anyone else in the last meeting?
qa.a: Leela spoke five times before anyone else got one turn.

qa.q: What does Leela's stopping mid-flow suggest Leela was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Leela was aware and a little self-conscious, trying to change a habit. Counting turns shows a genuine wish to make room.

qa.q: What did Leela do to make space for Vinita?
qa.a: Leela counted turns, stopped after the third and asked Vinita directly for input. Leela then stayed quiet until Vinita had finished.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when Leela asked "What do you think?"
qa.a: Vinita probably felt valued and invited, since Vinita sat up and gave a real concern. Being asked directly made it easy to speak.

grounding: A person who tends to talk a lot counts their own turns and asks a team member for input, making space for others.

passage:
I'm Salma, and I'm the person who fills every silence. In my first year at the agency, my manager told me kindly, "You have great ideas, but others need room." I felt a flush, then I got curious.
Now, in every meeting I keep a small tally on my notepad. When I reach three marks, I stop and ask someone else. Yesterday I looked at Gopika, our newest designer, who had said nothing for half an hour. "Gopika, you've been looking at that mockup. What do you see?" Gopika gave two points that changed our whole plan.
It is a habit I'm still learning, and it matters more because I'm senior.

qa.q: How many marks does Salma reach before stopping to ask someone else?
qa.a: Salma stops and asks someone else at three marks.

qa.q: What did Salma feel when the manager said others need room?
qa.a: Salma felt a flush of embarrassment and then curiosity. The comment was kind, so Salma treated it as something to work on.

qa.q: What small habit did Salma build to make space?
qa.a: Salma keeps a tally of turns on a notepad and, at three marks, stops and asks someone else. That turned the advice into a routine.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt when Salma asked what Gopika saw?
qa.a: Gopika probably felt invited and valued, since a direct question after half an hour of silence made room to speak. The two points changed the plan.

grounding: A person who talks a lot counts their own turns and asks the newest team member for input, making space for others.

passage:
Team lead's note, quarterly review
Kavitha, one of our strongest designers, has always spoken the most in meetings: quick, full of ideas, often answering questions meant for others. Last month in her feedback, I mentioned that newer team members like Swati rarely spoke when she was in the room.
Kavitha took it seriously. In today's review she kept a small tally on her notepad: each time she spoke, one line. After four lines she stopped and asked, "Swati, you worked on the checkout flow. What did you notice?"
Swati hesitated, then gave the best observation of the meeting: users were abandoning the page at the address step.
After the meeting, Kavitha told me the tally felt silly at first but useful. "I didn't realise how much space I was taking."
What I will do next: I will ask Kavitha to mentor Swati on the checkout redesign.

qa.q: What did Kavitha keep on her notepad?
qa.a: She kept a small tally, one line each time she spoke.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling after the meeting?
qa.a: Kavitha felt a little surprised and self-conscious at how much space she'd been taking, but pleased the tally helped.

qa.q: Why does Kavitha's habit matter, especially for someone like her?
qa.a: As a strong, dominant speaker, counting turns and asking quieter colleagues for input makes room for ideas that would otherwise be lost.

qa.q: How might Swati have experienced being asked directly?
qa.a: Swati probably felt nervous but valued, finally given room to share the best observation of the meeting.

grounding: An adult's note shows a talkative person counting her turns and asking a quieter colleague for input, making space.

passage:
Tuesday
Tried the experiment today. In the planning meeting I made a little mark in my notebook each time I talked. I've always been the "ideas guy", the one who fills silences. By the half-hour mark I had eleven marks. Eleven. Tarun had zero. Two others had one each.
I felt my face go warm. I'm a team lead now; when I talk, people stop.
So I stopped. I said, "Tarun, you've been quiet. What do you think about the vendor plan?"
He looked startled. Then he said the vendor had missed two deadlines last year and we should have a backup. Nobody had mentioned it. Least of all me.
It's strange: talking less made me feel more like a leader, not less.
Goal for Thursday: under six marks.
Hemant

qa.q: How many marks did Hemant have by the half-hour mark?
qa.a: By the half-hour mark Hemant had eleven marks.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he saw the marks?
qa.a: Hemant felt embarrassed, face going warm, realising how much airtime a team lead had been taking.

qa.q: What small habit could others borrow from Hemant?
qa.a: Keep a quick tally of your own turns, and when it's high, ask a quiet colleague a direct question.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Hemant asked him?
qa.a: Tarun was startled, then probably pleased and valued, since his point about the vendor turned out to be important.

grounding: A person who talks a lot counts their own turns and asks others for input, a habit that matters more as a senior.

Sahil: hey Vidya, quick question about today's meeting
Vidya: sure
Sahil: be honest. did I talk too much?
Vidya: ...honestly? a bit
Sahil: how much is a bit
Vidya: you asked for ideas and then answered your own question twice 😅
Sahil: ugh. yes. I did that
Vidya: it's ok. you're the manager, so when you speak first, everyone just agrees
Sahil: that's what I'm worried about. new plan: next meeting I'll ask the question and wait. and I'll go last
Vidya: that would help. Maya had a good idea today but didn't say it
Sahil: can you ask her to bring it on Monday? I'll keep quiet till she's done
Vidya: deal 🙂

qa.q: What did Vidya say Sahil did twice?
qa.a: Sahil asked for ideas and then answered the question twice.

qa.q: What was Sahil worried about?
qa.a: Sahil was worried that, as the manager, everyone just agrees when the manager speaks first, so real ideas get lost.

qa.q: What plan did Sahil make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Sahil will ask the question, wait and speak last, so others share ideas before hearing the manager's view.

qa.q: How might Maya feel with room to speak on Monday?
qa.a: Maya would likely feel encouraged and valued, finally able to share the good idea that was held back.

grounding: A manager who talks a lot checks their own airtime and plans to wait and speak last, since seniority makes space matter more.

passage: At the milk cooperative office near Anand, Wasim had a habit his old mentor once pointed out: he talked the most in every meeting. Now, as the new secretary, he kept a small tally in the margin of his notebook. By half past ten the monthly meeting stood at: Wasim, nine lines. Shalini ben, who ran the evening collection, one. The three older members, two each. Wasim looked at the tally, stopped mid-sentence and turned. "Shalini ben, you're at the counter every evening. What are we missing?" Shalini hesitated, then said the chilling unit had shut off twice last week around seven, when the power dipped, and nobody had written it down. The room went quiet. Nobody else had known. They spent the next half hour on a backup plan. When the meeting ended, the tally read: Wasim, eleven; Shalini ben, seven. He underlined it.

qa.q: How many lines had Wasim spoken by half past ten?
qa.a: Nine lines.

qa.q: Why did Wasim stop mid-sentence after checking his tally?
qa.a: Wasim felt a jolt of awareness, a little uncomfortable, seeing how much of the airtime he had taken as secretary.

qa.q: What habit is Wasim building, and why does it matter in his role?
qa.a: Counting his own turns and inviting quieter members in; as secretary his voice carries weight, so making space brings out problems others see.

qa.q: What was it like for Shalini ben to be asked directly?
qa.a: She hesitated at first, but the direct question gave her room to raise the chilling unit problem nobody else knew about.

grounding: Shows a person who tends to talk a lot counting his own turns and asking a quieter member for input, which brings out a hidden problem.
